steps: Resultant force: F = ma (N = kg × m/s²). Rearrange to find a = F/m or m = F/a
Momentum (HT): p = mv (kg m/s). Conservation: total momentum before = total momentum after
Force from momentum change (HT): F = Δp ÷ Δt. Longer time = smaller force
Wave speed: v = f × λ. Rearrange to f = v/λ or λ = v/f
method_card.title: Newton's Laws, Momentum and Waves
method_card.content:
Three equation families run this lesson.

F = ma: resultant force = mass × acceleration. A zero resultant force means constant speed (Newton's first law); a non-zero resultant causes acceleration (second law).

Momentum: p = mv, measured in kg m/s, and it is conserved in a closed system. The force from a momentum change is F = Δp ÷ Δt, so a longer collision time gives a smaller force. That is why crumple zones save lives.

Wave speed: v = f × λ. Convert any wavelength to metres before substituting.

exam_context.frequency: High: F = ma and wave speed appear in most papers

gold.display: A crumple zone extends a collision from 0.05 s to 0.25 s. The driver's change in momentum is 900 kg m/s. Calculate the force WITH the crumple zone in newtons.

misconceptions.message: With the crumple zone use the longer time, 0.25 s: F = 900 ÷ 0.25 = 3,600 N. Using 0.05 s gives 18,000 N, the force without the zone.
Force is Δp ÷ Δt = 900 ÷ 0.25 = 3,600 N. Multiplying by the time gives 225, which is wrong.

gold.hint: Use the longer time, 0.25 s, in F = Δp ÷ Δt.

guided_steps.hint: The change in momentum given.
guided_steps.say: Force from a momentum change: F = Δp ÷ Δt. The crumple zone means use the LONGER time, 0.25 s.

guided_steps.pre: Time with the crumple zone, Δt =
guided_steps.hint: Use the longer time, 0.25 s, not 0.05 s.
Divide the momentum change by the longer time.
guided_steps.done: F = 3,600 N with the crumple zone.

guided_steps.hint: Divide by the shorter time 0.05 s.
guided_steps.say: Compare with no crumple zone, where the time is only 0.05 s:
guided_steps.done: Without the zone the force is 18,000 N. The crumple zone cuts it to 3,600 N.

gold.display: A 60 kg astronaut pushes off a wall with a force of 120 N for 0.5 s. Calculate their final speed (starting from rest).

misconceptions.message: Impulse = F × t = 120 × 0.5 = 60 N s. That is the change in momentum, not the speed. Divide by mass: v = 60 ÷ 60 = 1 m/s.
You must include the time. v = (F × t) ÷ m = (120 × 0.5) ÷ 60 = 1 m/s. Using F ÷ m alone gives 2 m/s.

gold.hint: First find impulse F × t (the change in momentum), then divide by mass for speed.

guided_steps.hint: Multiply the force by the time.
guided_steps.say: Two steps. First the impulse, which equals the change in momentum: impulse = F × t.
guided_steps.done: The change in momentum is 60 N s.

guided_steps.hint: Divide the change in momentum by the mass.
guided_steps.say: Now the speed from the change in momentum: v = Δp ÷ m.

guided_steps.hint: Multiply mass by speed to get back the change in momentum.
guided_steps.done: Returns Δp = 60 N s, matching the impulse. Correct.

gold.display: Two trolleys (masses 2 kg and 3 kg) are pushed together at rest. After separation, the 2 kg trolley moves at 3 m/s. Calculate the speed of the 3 kg trolley in m/s (give the magnitude).

misconceptions.message: 6 kg m/s is the momentum of the 3 kg trolley, not its speed. Divide by its mass: v = 6 ÷ 3 = 2 m/s.
The trolleys do not share the same speed because their masses differ. Momentum is conserved: 2 × 3 = 3 × v, so v = 6 ÷ 3 = 2 m/s.

gold.hint: Total momentum stays 0: the 3 kg trolley carries the same momentum as the 2 kg one, the other way.

guided_steps.hint: Multiply its mass by its speed.
guided_steps.say: Both trolleys start at rest, so the total momentum is 0 and must stay 0. Momentum of the 2 kg trolley after: mass × speed.
guided_steps.done: The 2 kg trolley carries 6 kg m/s.

guided_steps.hint: Divide the momentum by the 3 kg mass.
guided_steps.say: To keep the total at 0, the 3 kg trolley must carry the same 6 kg m/s the other way: v = 6 ÷ mass.

guided_steps.hint: Multiply the 3 kg mass by its speed.
guided_steps.done: The 3 kg trolley carries 6 kg m/s, balancing the other. Total = 0. Correct.

bronze.display: A 5 kg object accelerates at 4 m/s². Calculate the resultant force acting on it.

misconceptions.message: F = m × a means multiply, not add. F = 5 × 4 = 20 N.

bronze.hint: Use F = m × a: multiply the mass by the acceleration.

guided_steps.hint: It is the mass given in the question.
guided_steps.say: Choose the equation. A force from mass and acceleration means F = m × a.

guided_steps.hint: It is the acceleration given in the question.
Multiply mass by acceleration.
guided_steps.say: Both values are already in base units, so substitute straight in.

guided_steps.hint: Divide the force by the mass to get back the acceleration.
guided_steps.done: That returns a = 4 m/s², so F = 20 N is right.

bronze.display: A 1,200 kg car accelerates at 3 m/s². Calculate the resultant force in newtons.

misconceptions.message: F = m × a means multiply: F = 1200 × 3 = 3,600 N. Adding gives 1203, which is wrong.

bronze.hint: Use F = m × a: multiply the mass by the acceleration.

guided_steps.hint: The mass given.
guided_steps.say: A force from mass and acceleration: F = m × a.

guided_steps.hint: The acceleration given.
Multiply mass by acceleration.
guided_steps.say: Values already in base units, substitute in.

guided_steps.hint: Divide force by mass.

bronze.display: A wave has a frequency of 5 Hz and wavelength 0.04 m. Calculate its speed.
bronze.question: A wave has a frequency of 5 Hz and wavelength 0.04 m. Calculate its speed.

misconceptions.message: Wave speed multiplies: v = f × λ = 5 × 0.04 = 0.2 m/s. Dividing gives 125, which is wrong.

bronze.hint: Use v = f × λ: multiply frequency by wavelength.

guided_steps.hint: The frequency given.
guided_steps.say: Wave speed links frequency and wavelength: v = f × λ.

guided_steps.hint: The wavelength given, in metres.
guided_steps.say: The wavelength is 0.04 m, already in metres, so no conversion.

guided_steps.hint: Multiply frequency by wavelength.
Divide speed by frequency to get back the wavelength.

bronze.display: A wave travels at 340 m/s with a frequency of 170 Hz. Calculate its wavelength.
bronze.question: A wave travels at 340 m/s with a frequency of 170 Hz. Calculate its wavelength.

misconceptions.message: Rearrange to λ = v ÷ f = 340 ÷ 170 = 2 m. Multiplying gives 57,800, far too big.

bronze.hint: Rearrange v = f × λ to λ = v ÷ f, then divide.

guided_steps.hint: The speed given.
guided_steps.say: Rearrange v = f × λ to make wavelength the subject: λ = v ÷ f.

guided_steps.hint: The frequency given.
Divide speed by frequency.
Multiply frequency by wavelength to get back the speed.

bronze.display: A resultant force of 600 N acts on a 200 kg object. Calculate the acceleration.

misconceptions.message: Rearrange to a = F ÷ m = 600 ÷ 200 = 3 m/s². Multiplying gives 120,000, which is wrong.

bronze.hint: Rearrange F = m × a to a = F ÷ m, then divide.

guided_steps.hint: The force given.
guided_steps.say: Rearrange F = m × a to make acceleration the subject: a = F ÷ m.

guided_steps.hint: The mass given.
Divide force by mass.
Multiply mass by acceleration to get back the force.

bronze.display: Calculate the momentum of a 70 kg person running at 5 m/s.

misconceptions.message: Momentum multiplies: p = m × v = 70 × 5 = 350 kg m/s. Adding gives 75, which is wrong.

bronze.hint: Use p = m × v: multiply mass by velocity.

guided_steps.hint: The mass given.
guided_steps.say: Momentum links mass and velocity: p = m × v.

guided_steps.hint: The speed given.
Multiply mass by velocity.
Divide momentum by mass to get back the velocity.

silver.display: A radio wave travels at 3 × 10⁸ m/s with a wavelength of 300 m. Calculate the frequency in Hz.
silver.question: A radio wave travels at 3 × 10⁸ m/s with a wavelength of 300 m. Calculate the frequency in Hz.

misconceptions.message: Frequency is f = v ÷ λ = 3×10⁸ ÷ 300 = 1×10⁶ Hz. Multiplying gives 9×10¹⁰, far too large.

silver.hint: Rearrange to f = v ÷ λ, then divide, keeping the power of ten.

guided_steps.hint: 3 divided by 300.
guided_steps.say: Rearrange v = f × λ for frequency: f = v ÷ λ. The wavelength 300 m is already in metres.

guided_steps.hint: Multiply frequency by wavelength to get back the speed.

silver.display: A 1,000 kg car brakes from 20 m/s to rest. Calculate the change in momentum.

misconceptions.message: Change in momentum is m × Δv = 1000 × 20 = 20,000 kg m/s. Adding the numbers gives 1020, which is wrong.

silver.hint: Change in velocity is 20 m/s (down to rest); use Δp = m × Δv.

guided_steps.hint: The mass given.
guided_steps.say: Change in momentum: Δp = m × Δv. The car brakes from 20 m/s to rest, so Δv = 20 m/s.

guided_steps.hint: From 20 m/s down to 0 is a change of 20.
Multiply mass by the change in velocity.
Divide by mass to get back the change in velocity.

silver.display: A resultant force of 1,500 N acts on a vehicle and causes an acceleration of 2.5 m/s². Calculate the mass of the vehicle.

misconceptions.message: Rearrange to m = F ÷ a = 1500 ÷ 2.5 = 600 kg. Multiplying gives 3750, which is wrong.

silver.hint: Rearrange F = m × a to m = F ÷ a, then divide.

guided_steps.hint: The force given.
guided_steps.say: Rearrange F = m × a for mass: m = F ÷ a.

guided_steps.hint: The acceleration given.
Divide force by acceleration.
Multiply mass by acceleration to get back the force.

silver.display: A driver's change in momentum during a crash is 900 kg m/s, occurring over 0.05 s. Calculate the force on the driver.

misconceptions.message: Force is Δp ÷ Δt = 900 ÷ 0.05 = 18,000 N. Multiplying by the time gives 45, which is wrong.

silver.hint: Use F = Δp ÷ Δt: divide the momentum change by the time.

guided_steps.hint: The change in momentum given.
guided_steps.say: Force from a momentum change: F = Δp ÷ Δt.

guided_steps.hint: The collision time given, in seconds.
Divide the momentum change by the time.
Multiply force by time to get back the momentum change.

problem_bank.bronze_description: One equation, all values already in base units. Write it, substitute, compute, state the unit.
problem_bank.silver_description: Rearrange the equation first, or handle a value in standard form, then substitute and compute.
problem_bank.gold_description: Chain two ideas: impulse then speed, or conservation of momentum, working through more than one step.

A sound wave has a frequency of 440 Hz and a wavelength of 0.77 m. Calculate its speed.

bronze.title: Bronze: one equation, straight in
steps: Pick the equation the quantities point to: F = m × a for forces, v = f × λ for waves, p = m × v for momentum.
The values are already in base units (kg, m/s, m, s), so substitute them straight in.
Compute, then write the answer with its unit (N, m/s, m, kg m/s).

example.question: A 4 kg mass accelerates at 5 m/s². Calculate the resultant force.

silver.title: Silver: rearrange, then substitute
steps: The quantity you want is not the subject yet. Rearrange first: from F = m × a you get a = F ÷ m or m = F ÷ a; from v = f × λ you get f = v ÷ λ or λ = v ÷ f.
Large or small numbers may be in standard form. Divide the front numbers, keep the power of ten, then write it out.
Substitute, compute, and state the unit.

example.question: A wave travels at 480 m/s with a frequency of 160 Hz. Calculate its wavelength.

steps.label: Rearrange
steps.content: v = f × λ, so λ = v ÷ f

gold.title: Gold: chain two steps
steps: Gold problems need two moves. A common chain: impulse (F × t) gives the change in momentum, then divide by mass for the speed.
Or use conservation of momentum: total momentum before = total momentum after. If everything starts at rest, the total is zero, so the two parts carry equal and opposite momentum.
Finish the second step and state the unit.

example.question: A 0.2 kg ball is pushed from rest by a 6 N force for 0.5 s. Calculate its final speed.

opener.label: Before any equations
opener.display:
You give two shopping trolleys the SAME shove.
Empty trolley: 10 kg. Full of bricks: 50 kg.

steps.pre: Which speeds up more, the 10 kg or the 50 kg? Type its mass:
steps.hint: The lighter one is easier to get moving.
steps.say: No physics yet, just instinct. One shove, two trolleys, which shoots off faster?

steps.hint: Divide the force by the mass.
steps.say: Now put a number on it. The shove is a force of 100 N. Acceleration = force ÷ mass. For the empty trolley:

steps.hint: Divide the force by the mass.

steps.say: You just used F = ma, rearranged to a = F ÷ m. Same force, but the 10 kg trolley gets 10 m/s² and the 50 kg one only 2 m/s². More mass, less acceleration. That one equation drives most of this lesson.

bronze.display: A 3 kg ball accelerates at 6 m/s². Calculate the resultant force.
bronze.label: Together: your first one

steps.say: The move: pick the equation, put the numbers in, compute. Equation: F = m × a.

steps.hint: Divide force by mass to get back the acceleration.
steps.done: Returns 6 m/s². Correct. That was the whole move: substitute and compute.

silver.display: A wave travels at 320 m/s with a frequency of 80 Hz. Calculate its wavelength.
silver.label: Together: the silver move

steps.say: The new move: rearrange first. v = f × λ, so λ = v ÷ f.

steps.hint: Multiply frequency by wavelength to get back the speed.
steps.done: Returns 320 m/s. Correct. The one new move was rearranging before substituting.

gold.display: A 2 kg trolley speeds up from 3 m/s to 8 m/s in 0.5 s. Calculate the change in momentum, then the resultant force.
gold.label: Together: the gold move

steps.hint: Subtract the starting speed from the final speed.
steps.say: Gold problems chain two equations. First the change in momentum: Δp = m × Δv.

steps.hint: Multiply mass by the change in velocity.
Divide the momentum change by the time.
Multiply force by time to get back Δp.
steps.done: Returns Δp = 10 kg m/s. Correct. The gold move was chaining two equations.
